summary: This Best Current Practice defines a syntax called a language-range for listing a user's language preferences, and two ways to match those against language tags: filtering, which returns a set, and lookup, which returns one tag. With RFC 4646 it replaced RFC 3066.

plainLanguage.summary:
RFC 4647 explains how to turn a person's list of preferred languages into a content choice. It defines a language range, the pattern a preference is written as, and two ways to compare ranges with the language tags attached to content.

Filtering returns every tag that matches, so it suits a search. Lookup returns the one tag that matches best, so it suits an error message or a template. The two schemes treat a range differently, so a protocol has to say which one it uses.

questions: what is the difference between filtering and lookup
subtitle: How a list of language preferences is matched against the language tags on offer.

tldr.problem: An application that can serve content in several languages needs a way to turn a user's list of language preferences into a choice. Preferences are written differently from the tags attached to the content, and the two are not compared the same way.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4647 defines a language range as the way to write a preference, and defines two ways to compare ranges with language tags. Filtering returns a set of matching tags. Lookup returns the single tag that matches best.
tldr.outcome: The document is Best Current Practice 47 and, together with RFC 4646, replaces RFC 3066. Every protocol that uses the scheme has to say which matching it uses and what it does when nothing matches.

facts.label: Filtering returns
facts.value: A set of matching tags, possibly empty

facts.label: Lookup returns
facts.value: One matching tag, or the default

today: RFC 4647 is Best Current Practice 47, published in September 2006. It replaced RFC 3066, which had replaced RFC 1766, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated. The document requires any protocol that uses language tag matching to say which matching scheme it uses and what it returns when nothing matches.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Language tags identify a language for communication, and applications that use them often need to match those tags against a user's preferences. The HTTP Accept-Language header is one example: it carries the preferences, and the server uses them to choose content.

RFC 4647 defines a syntax for those preferences, called a language range, and several schemes for matching ranges against language tags. It is Best Current Practice 47. Together with RFC 4646 it replaces RFC 3066, which had replaced RFC 1766.

The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: This document answers one question: how does a server turn a list of language preferences into the right page? It defines the way preferences are written and the rules for comparing them with what is on offer.

sections.title: The Language Range
sections.content:
A language range names a set of language tags that share certain attributes. Like a language tag, it is a sequence of subtags separated by hyphens, and each subtag must be either a sequence of ASCII letters and digits or the single character '*', which matches any sequence of subtags.

Two kinds exist. A basic language range has the same syntax as the language tag of RFC 3066, or is just '*': language-range = (1*8ALPHA *("-" 1*8alphanum)) / "*". An extended language range allows a wildcard in any position: extended-language-range = (1*8ALPHA / "*") *("-" (1*8alphanum / "*")). An extended range lets a user ask for tags that carry a particular subtag without naming the ones in between, such as every tag with the region subtag CH.

Language tags and ranges are case-insensitive. Capitalisation conventions exist for some subtags, but they carry no meaning, and all matching is done without regard to case.

A language priority list is a prioritized list of ranges. A speaker of Breton in France can write br, fr to say that Breton is preferred and French is the fallback. The document does not define the syntax of such a list, because that belongs to the protocol that carries it.
sections.plainLanguage: A preference is written as a hyphenated pattern, much like the language tag on the content itself. The pattern '*' stands for any part. There are two forms: the basic form, used by older protocols, and the extended form, which allows a wildcard anywhere.

sections.title: Choosing a Matching Scheme
sections.content:
Two kinds of scheme are defined. A scheme that produces zero or more matching tags is called filtering. A scheme that produces exactly one match for a given request is called lookup. Three concrete schemes are described: basic filtering, extended filtering and lookup.

Filtering suits work that wants a set, such as limiting a search to documents tagged as being in French. Lookup suits work that must return one item, such as choosing the text of an error message that goes into a protocol header. Lookup has to return something even when nothing matches, so it needs a defined default.

Language tag matching is a tool, not a whole procedure, and the document requires any protocol that uses it to state which types of matching it uses, whether the operation returns one result or a set, and, for lookup, what the default is when no tag matches. The default could be an error, an empty value, a protocol-defined or implementation-defined item, or the tag i-default from RFC 2277.

An implementation does not have to understand the meaning of the subtags or consult the IANA Language Subtag Registry, which keeps the work simple. It is encouraged to use the registry to canonicalize tags, so that grandfathered and obsolete forms map onto modern equivalents. An implementation that canonicalizes ranges must either match against both the canonical and the original form, or canonicalize each tag as well.
sections.plainLanguage:
Two schemes are on offer. Filtering finds every tag that fits and is used when a list of results is wanted. Lookup finds the one tag that fits best and is used when only one answer can be given.

A protocol that uses either has to say which one it uses and what to do when nothing matches, because the two schemes read a range differently: filtering treats a range as the least specific tag that is good enough, lookup treats it as the most specific tag that is good enough.

sections.title: Filtering
sections.content:
In filtering, each range in the priority list stands for the least specific tag that is acceptable, so every matching tag has at least as many subtags as the range, and every non-wildcard subtag in the range appears in every matching tag. With the range de-CH (German as used in Switzerland), a tag such as de-CH-1996 matches but de does not, because the CH subtag is missing.

Basic filtering compares ranges to tags by string prefix. A range matches a tag if, ignoring case, it equals the tag exactly, or if it equals a prefix of the tag and the character after that prefix is a hyphen. So de-de matches de-DE-1996, but not de-Deva or de-Latn-DE. The range '*' matches any tag; a protocol may add its own rules, and HTTP/1.1 says that '*' matches only languages not matched by any other range in the header. Basic filtering is identical to the matching described in RFC 3066.

When the priority list holds more than one range, the content is typically ordered by descending preference, but it may be unordered. Filtering suits applying a style to parts of a document, showing the documents that contain keywords in certain languages, selecting email in certain languages, or selecting audio files in a language.

One warning: a shared prefix does not prove that two languages are mutually intelligible, so a filter that returns a set of tags is not a promise that the reader understands them all.
sections.plainLanguage: Filtering finds every tag that matches a preference. A range such as de-CH matches tags that start with German and Switzerland, such as de-CH-1996, but not plain de. The comparison is a plain prefix test, ignoring case.

sections.title: Extended Filtering
sections.content:
Extended filtering compares an extended range to a tag subtag by subtag. Both are split on the hyphen. Two subtags match if they are the same ignoring case, or if the range's subtag is the wildcard '*'.

The comparison starts at the first subtag of each. If those do not match, the comparison fails. After that, while the range still has subtags left: a wildcard in the range is skipped; if the tag has no subtags left, the comparison fails; if the current subtags match, both lists move on; if the tag's current subtag is a singleton, a single letter or digit that includes the private-use subtag x, the comparison fails; otherwise the tag's list moves on and the loop continues. When the range has no subtags left, the comparison succeeds.

Subtags not named by the range, including any at the end of it, are treated as if they were wildcards. The range de-*-DE, or its synonym de-DE, therefore matches de-DE, de-de, de-Latn-DE, de-Latf-DE, de-DE-x-goethe, de-Latn-DE-1996 and de-Deva-DE. It does not match de, because DE is missing, nor de-x-DE, because the singleton x comes before DE, nor de-Deva, because Deva is not DE.

Because RFC 4646 fixes the type of each subtag by its position, a subtag in a range can only match that type in a tag: Latn is always a script subtag, and a two-letter subtag in the first position is a language while the same two letters later are a region. That is why a wildcard in the first position is significant but is ignored in all others.
sections.plainLanguage:
Extended filtering compares the range and the tag piece by piece instead of as plain strings. A wildcard in the range stands in for any subtags in the tag at that point, so de-*-DE matches German tags for Germany even when a script subtag sits in between.

Two things end the comparison: the range runs out of subtags, which is a match, or the tag's current subtag is a single letter or digit that does not match the range, which fails.

sections.title: Lookup
sections.content:
Lookup finds the single tag that best matches the priority list. Each range is considered in priority order, and here the range stands for the most specific tag that is acceptable. The first match found is the closest one and is returned. So a lookup for de-ch can return de or de-CH, but never de-CH-1996.

The search narrows the range step by step. Single-letter and single-digit subtags, including x and the subtags that introduce extensions, are removed along with the subtag just before them. Starting from zh-Hant-CN-x-private1-private2, the search looks for zh-Hant-CN-x-private1-private2, then zh-Hant-CN-x-private1, then zh-Hant-CN, then zh-Hant, then zh, and finally the default.

Without the fallback, the default would be returned as soon as the exact content was missing. With it, a result closer to the request can be given instead. Extensions and unrecognized private-use subtags sit at the end of the tag, so they are removed first and rarely get in the way. An implementation may remove them before the lookup, provided it removes them from the tags too, but it should not modify subtags in the content it returns, because that discards information others may need.

The range '*' matches any tag, but on its own it does not say which tag is best. If other ranges follow it, '*' is skipped. If it is the only range, or nothing else follows it, the default is computed and returned. If a protocol accepts extended ranges it must define which item is returned when more than one matches, because a single result is required. One option is to map extended ranges to basic ranges; another is to return the matching tag that comes first in ASCII order, so a range of *-CH over de-CH, fr-CH and it-CH returns de-CH.
sections.plainLanguage:
Lookup returns one tag. It starts with the most specific range in the list and works down to less specific ones until it finds a match, so a request for de-CH can be answered with plain de when nothing more specific exists.

Every lookup needs a rule for the case where nothing matches at all. The protocol has to supply one, and the RFC lists several choices.

sections.title: Choosing Language Ranges
sections.content:
Most schemes do not look at what the subtags mean. They compare strings, ignoring case, so users are told to choose ranges that are well-formed valid language tags, with wildcards substituted where appropriate in extended ranges.

Users should avoid subtags that add nothing. When filtering, fewer subtags match more content. When lookup is used, unnecessary subtags can push out better content: the range de-Latn-DE returns content tagged de instead of content tagged de-DE, even though the latter is the better match.

Whether a subtag distinguishes anything depends on the request. A reader of both Simplified and Traditional Chinese who prefers Simplified might use zh for filtering, to catch everything readable, and zh-Hans for lookup, to get the preferred form when it exists. The list zh-Hans, zh serves both schemes well. When the scheme is not known, the most specific range should come first, with shorter prefixes later, so that filtering still returns a complete set.

Many languages are written in one script, and the registry records that in the Suppress-Script field. For those, script subtags should not be used to build a range, so en-Latn is usually inappropriate. Extensions and most private-use subtags describe attributes that have nothing to do with matching, and users are told to avoid them in ranges because they get in the way of selection.

Private-use subtags need agreement between the parties that use them. Their value and meaning are undefined, they are useless for exchange without prior arrangement, and matching them can return unpredictable content. The length limits that apply to language tags apply to ranges too.
sections.plainLanguage:
The shorter the range, the more content it matches, so extra subtags are worth adding only when they change the answer. A range such as de-Latn-DE can stop a lookup from reaching the better de-DE content.

Users should also avoid private-use subtags, because their meaning is undefined and they only work between parties that have agreed on them in advance.

sections.title: Security and Character Set Considerations
sections.content:
Language ranges used in content negotiation might be used to infer the nationality of the sender, and so identify targets for surveillance. Unique or highly unusual ranges, or unusual combinations of ranges, might be used to track the activities of a specific individual. This is the general problem that whatever you send is visible to the receiving party. How large the threat is, and what to do about it, is left to each application or protocol.

Language tags permit only the characters A-Z, a-z, 0-9 and HYPHEN-MINUS (%x2D). Language ranges also use ASTERISK (%x2A). These characters are present in most character sets, so presenting or exchanging tags and ranges should not be constrained by character set issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The ranges a person sends can reveal where they are from, and unusual ones can be used to follow one person across requests. That is a general property of anything you send, and the RFC leaves the size of the risk to each application.

items.title: Start at the first subtag
items.text: If the first subtag of the range and the first subtag of the tag do not match, the comparison fails.

items.title: Wildcards are skipped
items.text: A wildcard in the range is passed over, and the tag's subtags keep moving forward.

items.title: A singleton stops the match
items.text: If the tag's current subtag is a single letter or digit and it does not match the range, the comparison fails.

items.title: Unnamed subtags act as wildcards
items.text: Subtags the range does not name, including any at its end, are treated as wildcards.
